title: After 175 live trades, my crypto bot went from a 1.77 profit factor into a 50% drawdown. Here’s what broke
author: Trader_for_earner
selftext:
I’ve been live paper/micro-trading a systematic bot across about a dozen altcoins (UNI, SEI, APT, ADA, FIL, etc.) using fixed risk brackets, automated entry rules, and hard time stops. Through the first 104 trades, the bot was printing nicely—sitting at around a 56% win rate, a 1.77 profit factor, and up about 25R.

Then over the last 71 trades, performance completely fell off a cliff. The win rate collapsed down to 39%, the profit factor dropped to 0.68, and the system gave back more than half the peak gains. Since every single order and exit is tracked to a ledger, I dug into the logs to see what actually changed between the two regimes.

The biggest culprit wasn't bad entries—it was target starvation. In the first phase, crypto had clear directional expansions, so taking 1.5 to 2.0 ATR on a take-profit was routine (about a third of our trades hit full TP). But recently, volatility compressed into ugly chop. Price would push 0.7 or 0.8 ATR into profit, stall out shy of our limit order, and then slowly bleed back into our stop loss or get closed out at breakeven by our hard time stop. Our full TP hit rate plunged from 32% down to under 13%, while stop-outs jumped up to nearly 50%.

On top of that, directional asymmetry bit hard. During the run-up, our short momentum setups carried the entire account (64% win rate on shorts), easily masking the fact that our longs were already dragging. Once the broader market stopped trending down and started churning sideways, the shorts lost their follow-through, and pure breakout setups went 0 for 7. Meanwhile, our high-frequency VWAP deviation scalper got chopped to pieces because the bands compressed so tightly that commissions and small wicks ate away any statistical edge.

For those running automated intraday or swing bots in crypto: how do you deal with this kind of regime transition? Do you dynamically contract your profit targets when realized volatility or ATR drops into lower percentiles, or do you prefer to just shut down specific archetypes like breakouts entirely during chop? Also, how do you handle asymmetric bleeding on the long side when higher timeframes are in a macro downtrend?

Curious to hear how you guys protect against giving back months of steady alpha when the market shifts from clean trend to low-vol churn.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
The target starvation part is the interesting one. The TP is set in ATR at entry, but when ATR shrinks the move you need just isn't there anymore. I'd check the ATR percentile at entry and see if the 1.5-2 ATR target ever hit when ATR was in the bottom third, even in the first 104 trades. If it didn't, that's more of a filter than a target to shrink.

Also 71 trades isn't much to split by long/short and by setup, so I'd be careful fixing each piece separately.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
honest write-up, thanks for posting the bad half too.

one thing I'd check before fixing anything: add the two phases together. +25R over 104 trades, then giving back more than half of it over 71, leaves roughly +10 to +12R over 175 trades, so somewhere around 0.06-0.07R per trade. with a dozen alts often moving together, the real number of independent trades is a lot lower than 175. that total is very hard to tell apart from zero. so the question might not be "what broke" but "was the first phase ever an edge, or a good stretch".

second, the shorts carrying the account while alts were trending down is a big flag. in a falling market, random shorts make money too. compare your short entries against random shorts on the same coins and days with the same brackets. if random shorts with your exits did about as well, the first phase was the market, not the system.

on regime filters: be careful building one from these same 175 trades. it's easy to find an ATR percentile that would have switched off the bad stretch, but that's fitted to exactly the period you're looking at. if you add one, define it in advance using only data before each trade, and check whether the regime is actually predictable a few days ahead (is low vol today a decent predictor of low vol next week on your coins?). otherwise you'll just be turning the bot off right after the chop and back on right before the next one.

and 0 for 7 on breakouts is too few trades to conclude anything either way.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you logged every exit, because that's how you found target starvation instead of just blaming the entries. Switching off the setups that need expansion, like the breakouts and the tight-band scalper, when ATR sits in a low percentile is usually simpler than shrinking targets on the fly, since moving targets adds another knob to overfit. Whatever filter you pick, check that it also would have kept the good stretch intact and didn't just dodge the bad one. A drop over a few dozen trades can also be partly noise, so I'd want the filter to hold across more than one chop period. Cymetica's Backtest Labs includes fees and holds out the last part of the history, which helps with that kind of check.
